doc.title: Dick Spottswood interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 13, 2023

title: Finding Clarence Williams' Kansas City Man Blues in a barn
summary: At eleven or twelve he found a Clarence Williams Blue Five record at a Pennsylvania sale, not knowing Bechet's name, and later met other collectors around Washington.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I think the economic truism that supply and demand certainly applies to rare recordings and so forth. Do you have a memory of searching through bins and Salvation Army stuff, what has been some of the significant finds that you may recall?

I’ve been very fortunate in that respect over the years and have found many good records like that too. You know because like it occurred to me when I was young that I was only going to find the music I liked or the records I liked by going through used record bins because they weren’t for sale at retailers any longer. I was about twenty years too late for the music that really captured my imagination. So I still remember the first important record I ever found I was about eleven or twelve years old and I was with some relatives at some kind of a sale in a barn up in Central Pennsylvania and there were some old records and I thought well why don’t I look through these. I was a little kid with nothing else to do. And I pulled up a copy of the “Kansas City Man Blues” by Clarence Williams’ Blue Five. I had no idea who they were but it said blues on the other side too so I paid the dime or the quarter or whatever was required and got that record home and it turned out to be a monster. But I didn’t even know how to pronounce Sidney Bechet’s last name at that point. I just knew the music was good.
That’s a great story. Yeah, like oh who’s this, is this Sidney Bechet and what does he play?
Well his name wasn’t on the record. I didn’t learn that until later.
How many years later was it that you discovered that this was a valuable purchase?

Oh it didn’t take long. I don’t remember how that evolved. But as my interest in that music grew and I was able to articulate it a little better, you know I ran into other local people that played music and collected music. And you know I grew up in suburban

Washington, D.C. and that was a very cosmopolitan place. And no matter what your interests were if you poked around a little bit you could always find colleagues and enemies and other people that had to do with what you were interested in too.
